Reference: Castro-Vincenzi (2024)

Model Setting

The paper asks how the likelihood of extreme weather events shapes the spatial organization of firms, and how much firm-level adaptation can buffer the cost of climate change. The setting is the global car industry: multinational, multiplant firms that produce tradable goods in physical sites exposed to floods. Two adaptation margins are studied. Ex ante, firms choose where to locate plants and how much capacity to install in each. Ex post, multiplant firms reallocate production from disrupted to undisrupted plants, up to the capacity installed there. An event study on plant-level data for 2000 to 2019 shows that a severe flood near an assembly plant lowers its output persistently and that sibling plants of the same firm raise theirs. The paper then builds a static, quantitative, multiregion model in which a firm makes sunk capacity investments in many locations before local productivity shocks are realized, and afterwards chooses production flows from each plant to each market subject to the capacity constraints. The firm trades off proximity to large markets, low production and capacity costs, and resilience: because a plant can be an export platform for any market, holding capacity in several locations, and more capacity than is used in normal times, is a hedge against disruption of one plant.

The methodological contribution is that plant location is not treated as a combinatorial discrete choice with fixed costs. Capacity is continuous with a strictly positive marginal cost at zero, so a location is left empty when the expected shadow value of its first unit of capacity is below that cost. The resulting ex ante problem is a convex optimization problem, whose dual can be written as a conic program that standard solvers handle very quickly. The model is estimated on the 2019 geography of car production and combined with CMIP6 projections of extreme precipitation for 2035 to 2064. Under the high-emissions scenario SSP5-8.5, firms build more but smaller plants and hold more spare capacity, firm size and profits fall by 4 to 5 percent, and adaptation averts about one fifth of the profit loss. Consumers, however, are worse off with adaptation than without it, because the reorganization of production lowers the productivity and capacity of every variety at once.

Event-Study Evidence

The data are quarterly registrations of car models by assembly plant and country of sale from IHS Markit (354 brands, 77 countries of sale, 1,105 plants in 54 countries), matched to the Dartmouth Flood Observatory archive of large floods. A location is a first-level administrative unit (GAUL1). A plant is treated when a flood has its centroid within 100 kilometers; 77 percent of plants are treated at least once in the sample, but only in 2.4 percent of plant-quarters. The paper uses the difference-in-differences estimator of de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille (2022), which is robust to heterogeneous and dynamic effects. For plant iii first treated in period FiF_iFi​, and ℓ\ellℓ periods after that date:

DIDiℓ=Yi,Fi+ℓ−Yi,Fi−1−∑i′:Fi′>Fi+ℓ1∑i′:Fi′>Fi+ℓ1(Yi′,Fi+ℓ−Yi′,Fi−1)(1)DID_{i\ell}=Y_{i,F_i+\ell}-Y_{i,F_i-1}-\sum_{i':F_{i'}>F_i+\ell}\frac{1}{\sum_{i':F_{i'}>F_i+\ell}1}\left(Y_{i',F_i+\ell}-Y_{i',F_i-1}\right) \tag{1}DIDiℓ​=Yi,Fi​+ℓ​−Yi,Fi​−1​−i′:Fi′​>Fi​+ℓ∑​∑i′:Fi′​>Fi​+ℓ​11​(Yi′,Fi​+ℓ​−Yi′,Fi​−1​)(1)

where YYY is log plant production, Nℓ1N^1_{\ell}Nℓ1​ is the number of plants that reach ℓ\ellℓ periods after their first flood by the end of the sample TTT, and the control group consists of plants not yet treated at Fi+ℓF_i+\ellFi​+ℓ. Standard errors are clustered by GAUL1 unit.

  • Direct effect: production falls persistently and stabilizes about 20 quarters after the flood. The long-run average (quarters 20 to 40) is −0.34-0.34−0.34 log points for all floods, −0.69-0.69−0.69 for 100-year floods and −0.28-0.28−0.28 for 10-year floods.

  • Reallocation: plants that are never flooded themselves but produce at least one of the car models of a flooded sibling plant raise production by 0.460.460.46 log points in the long run. Firm-level production still falls by about 25 percent one year after the shock and recovers later, so the offset is partial.

  • Extensive margin: the probability that an existing plant stays active is unaffected, but the number of plants in a second-level unit falls by 0.090.090.09 log points, which suggests that new plants avoid flooded regions.

  • Robustness: controlling for floods at sibling plants gives −0.33-0.33−0.33, and distance thresholds between 25 and 200 kilometers give similar dynamics.

Ex Post Production Allocation

This is an optimal flow problem: a monopolist facing isoelastic demand in each market chooses both how much to sell and which plants to source from, with a capacity limit at each source. The multiplier νin\nu_{in}νin​ is the shadow value of capacity in location iii. It is also the opportunity cost of using a constrained plant, since a unit shipped to one market takes capacity away from the others. The profit-maximizing price and quantity in market jjj are:

Each market is served from the plant with the lowest delivered marginal cost, where the production cost of each plant is augmented by its shadow value of capacity. A market can be served by several plants at once, in which case the multipliers adjust until the augmented delivered costs are equal. Because the multipliers are common to all markets served by a plant, sourcing decisions are interdependent across markets even after capacity is installed, unlike in models with constant marginal costs.

Ex Ante Location and Capacity Choice

Before the shocks are realized the firm chooses capacities to maximize expected operating profits net of investment costs:

max⁡Cin≥0  Eεn[Πn(Cn,εn)]−∑i=1IαinCin(11)\max_{C_{in}\geq0}\;\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon_n}}\left[\Pi_n(\boldsymbol{C_n},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon_n})\right]-\sum_{i=1}^{I}\alpha_{in}C_{in} \tag{11}Cin​≥0max​Eεn​​[Πn​(Cn​,εn​)]−i=1∑I​αin​Cin​(11)

By the envelope theorem, the first-order condition for each location is:

Eεn[νin(Cn,εn)]≤αin(12)\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\varepsilon_n}}\left[\nu_{in}(\boldsymbol{C_n},\boldsymbol{\varepsilon_n})\right]\leq\alpha_{in} \tag{12}Eεn​​[νin​(Cn​,εn​)]≤αin​(12)

with equality if the firm builds a plant in iii. The firm invests until the expected shadow value of capacity equals its marginal cost. It builds no plant in iii when, at the optimal capacities elsewhere, the expected value of an infinitesimal plant is below fin′(0)f_{in}'(0)fin′​(0); this is how the model generates zeros, and therefore the extensive margin of plant location, without fixed costs. A positive capacity requires the constraint of plant iii to bind in a positive measure of states.

The same condition explains diversification and hedging. When a flood hits plant iii, its multiplier falls because the plant is less productive, while the multipliers of the firm's other plants weakly rise because their capacity becomes scarcer. A higher flood probability in iii puts more weight on low-multiplier states there, which lowers the expected return to capacity in iii and weakly raises it elsewhere, and capacities adjust until the condition holds again in every location. A plant whose capacity binds only when a sibling plant is disrupted still earns a positive expected shadow value, so the firm rationally installs capacity that is idle in normal times (spare capacity). In a world without shocks all installed capacity is used.

Convexity (Proposition 1)

Proposition 1 states that the ex ante problem is the maximization of a concave objective on a set defined by linear constraints. Since investment costs are convex and expectations preserve concavity, it suffices to show that operating profits are concave in capacities. Write f(q)f(q)f(q) for the objective of the ex post problem, which is concave in the vector of flows, and D(C)D(C)D(C) for the set of flows that are feasible under capacities CCC. Take two capacity vectors C1C^1C1 and C2C^2C2 with optimal flows q1q^1q1 and q2q^2q2, and a weight θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1)θ∈(0,1). The flow θq1+(1−θ)q2\theta q^1+(1-\theta)q^2θq1+(1−θ)q2 is feasible under the averaged capacities because the constraints are linear, so:

Π(θC1+(1−θ)C2,ε)=max⁡q∈D(θC1+(1−θ)C2)f(q)≥f(θq1+(1−θ)q2)≥θf(q1)+(1−θ)f(q2)=θΠ(C1,ε)+(1−θ)Π(C2,ε)(13)\begin{aligned} \Pi\left(\theta C^1+(1-\theta)C^2,\varepsilon\right)&=\max_{q\in D(\theta C^1+(1-\theta)C^2)}f(q)\geq f\left(\theta q^1+(1-\theta)q^2\right)\\ &\geq\theta f(q^1)+(1-\theta)f(q^2)=\theta\Pi(C^1,\varepsilon)+(1-\theta)\Pi(C^2,\varepsilon) \end{aligned} \tag{13}Π(θC1+(1−θ)C2,ε)​=q∈D(θC1+(1−θ)C2)max​f(q)≥f(θq1+(1−θ)q2)≥θf(q1)+(1−θ)f(q2)=θΠ(C1,ε)+(1−θ)Π(C2,ε)​(13)

Any local optimum is therefore global, the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions are sufficient, and Slater's condition gives strong duality. The interdependence across locations that makes fixed-cost models combinatorial and nonconvex (Tintelnot 2017; Arkolakis, Eckert and Shi 2023) is preserved here, but inside a convex program.

Two Locations and One Market

The appendix studies a case with one market of size one, unit wages, a common trade cost τ\tauτ, and two locations with productivities z1>z2>κz1z_1>z_2>\kappa z_1z1​>z2​>κz1​, where only location 1 is disrupted, with probability ppp and damage κ\kappaκ. Let ε1≥ε2\varepsilon_1\geq\varepsilon_2ε1​≥ε2​ be the realized productivities. The shadow value of capacity in the more productive plant is:

In the first case both capacities bind. In the second the better plant is full and the worse plant is used but not full, so one more unit of good capacity saves the cost difference between the two plants (the factor 1/ϕ1/\phi1/ϕ follows from the profit function and is omitted in the paper's display). In the third the better plant is full and the other is idle, and in the fourth the better plant has slack. If parameters are such that only the most productive plant is used in each state, plant 1 serves the market in normal times and plant 2 only when plant 1 is flooded, and the first-order conditions give:

C1∗=(α11−p+1ϕz1)−σ(σ−1σ)στ1−σ,C2∗=(α2p+1ϕz2)−σ(σ−1σ)στ1−σ(21)C_1^*=\left(\frac{\alpha_1}{1-p}+\frac{1}{\phi z_1}\right)^{-\sigma}\left(\frac{\sigma-1}{\sigma}\right)^{\sigma}\tau^{1-\sigma},\qquad C_2^*=\left(\frac{\alpha_2}{p}+\frac{1}{\phi z_2}\right)^{-\sigma}\left(\frac{\sigma-1}{\sigma}\right)^{\sigma}\tau^{1-\sigma} \tag{21}C1∗​=(1−pα1​​+ϕz1​1​)−σ(σσ−1​)στ1−σ,C2∗​=(pα2​​+ϕz2​1​)−σ(σσ−1​)στ1−σ(21)

Capacity behaves as if its cost were scaled up by the inverse of the probability with which it is used: a higher ppp shrinks the risky plant and enlarges the backup plant, which stands idle with probability 1−p1-p1−p. The appendix compares this model with a fixed-cost model calibrated to the same plant probabilities and plant sizes. A higher disruption probability moves plant location in the same direction in both. A mean-preserving spread of the shock sharply raises investment in the risky location in the fixed-cost model, because profits are convex in marginal cost and output is unbounded in the good state, whereas with capacity the response is non-monotonic and depends on the cost of capacity. Only the capacity model yields a plant size, spare capacity, markets served by several plants, and ex post spillovers across markets when market access changes.

Estimation: Trade Costs and Demand

Estimation uses 2019 data, with brands as firms, and proceeds in two steps. In the first step trade costs are parameterized as τij=(1+tariffij)ϕtardijϕdist\tau_{ij}=(1+\text{tariff}_{ij})^{\phi_{tar}}d_{ij}^{\phi_{dist}}τij​=(1+tariffij​)ϕtar​dijϕdist​​ and estimated from list prices of the same car model mmm made in the same plant and sold in different markets, using the pricing rule:

log⁡(pijm)=ϕtarlog⁡(1+tariffij)+ϕdistlog⁡dij+αim+αj+uijm(22)\log(p_{ijm})=\phi_{tar}\log(1+\text{tariff}_{ij})+\phi_{dist}\log d_{ij}+\alpha_{im}+\alpha_j+u_{ijm} \tag{22}log(pijm​)=ϕtar​log(1+tariffij​)+ϕdist​logdij​+αim​+αj​+uijm​(22)

The model-plant fixed effect αim\alpha_{im}αim​ absorbs the marginal cost, including the shadow value of capacity, and αj\alpha_jαj​ absorbs market-specific measurement error. The estimates are ϕtar=0.834\phi_{tar}=0.834ϕtar​=0.834 (standard error 0.075) and ϕdist=0.033\phi_{dist}=0.033ϕdist​=0.033 (0.004). Demand is a nested CES with an inner nest across the models of a brand, estimated with two share regressions:

where sjmns_{jmn}sjmn​ is the share of model mmm within brand nnn in market jjj, PjnP_{jn}Pjn​ is the brand-level price composite, and sjns_{jn}sjn​ is the brand's market share. Prices in the first regression are instrumented with tariffs, because prices are measured with error and marginal costs are not constant in this model. The elasticity is 4.3 across models of a brand and σ=2.6\sigma=2.6σ=2.6 across brands, and the home market coefficient is about 1.0. Estimation: Productivities, Capacity Costs and Flood Damages

The firm-location productivities and capacity costs cannot be recovered by inverting the model, so they are treated as structural errors with log-normal distributions whose means depend on observables:

Finz(zin)=log⁡N(Xin′δz+Gi′δw,ξz),Finα(αin)=log⁡N(Xin′δα,ξα)(25)F^z_{in}(z_{in})=\log\mathcal{N}\left(X_{in}'\delta^z+G_i'\delta^w,\xi^z\right),\qquad F^{\alpha}_{in}(\alpha_{in})=\log\mathcal{N}\left(X_{in}'\delta^{\alpha},\xi^{\alpha}\right) \tag{25}Finz​(zin​)=logN(Xin′​δz+Gi′​δw,ξz),Finα​(αin​)=logN(Xin′​δα,ξα)(25)

The vector XinX_{in}Xin​ contains a constant, local log GDP per capita, log population, log road density, a home-country dummy, log distance to the headquarters country and the share of available land; GiG_iGi​ are dummies for six country income groups, which subsume wages. The parameter vector Θ={δz,δα,δw,ξz,ξα,κ1,κ2}\Theta=\{\delta^z,\delta^{\alpha},\delta^w,\xi^z,\xi^{\alpha},\kappa_1,\kappa_2\}Θ={δz,δα,δw,ξz,ξα,κ1​,κ2​} is estimated by the simulated method of moments with 48 moments in three blocks. The first block interacts the elements of XinX_{in}Xin​ and GiG_iGi​ with log production log⁡Yin\log Y_{in}logYin​ and with the plant indicator DinD_{in}Din​, which pins down the spatial distribution of plants and output. The second block matches the firm-level distributions of total production and number of plants (means and squares of logs, percentiles, their joint moment) and the size of the largest plant and its gap to the second largest. The third block identifies the damage parameters: floods are simulated inside the model with probabilities of 10 and 1 percent, and the difference in log output of a plant with and without a flood, holding capacity fixed, is matched to the event-study estimates. A two-location simulation in the appendix illustrates why productivity and capacity-cost parameters are separately identified: average log production moves mostly with capacity costs, because firms are often capacity constrained, while the share of locations with a plant moves mostly with productivity.

  • Flood damages: κ1=0.227\kappa_1=0.227κ1​=0.227 and κ2=0.415\kappa_2=0.415κ2​=0.415, so productivity falls by about 75 percent after a 100-year flood and 60 percent after a 10-year flood.

  • Capacity costs: the coefficients are 0.0210.0210.021 on log population, 0.0090.0090.009 on log road density, 0.0480.0480.048 on log GDP per capita, −0.277-0.277−0.277 on the home dummy, 0.0500.0500.050 on log distance to headquarters and −0.125-0.125−0.125 on land availability. Capacity is about 24 percent cheaper in the headquarters country and cheaper where land is abundant.

  • Productivity: the coefficients are 0.0340.0340.034 on log population, 0.0250.0250.025 on log road density, 0.0710.0710.071 on log GDP per capita, 0.2270.2270.227 on the home dummy, −0.042-0.042−0.042 on log distance to headquarters and −0.052-0.052−0.052 on land availability. The dispersion parameters are small (ξz=0.011\xi^z=0.011ξz=0.011, ξα=0.001\xi^{\alpha}=0.001ξα=0.001).

  • Fit: the average firm has 5.33 plants in the model and 5.26 in the data; average output per plant is 90 thousand cars against 100 thousand; the standard deviation of log plant size is 2.69 against 2.75. Sales by country are matched closely although they are not targeted. The model overstates the gap between the largest and second-largest plant and the effect of 10-year floods, and its plant size distribution is right-skewed while the data are left-skewed.

Counterfactuals: Climate Change

Flood risk is measured as the annual probability, in 2035 to 2064, of five-day rainfall above the local historical 10-year and 100-year thresholds, from a CMIP6 multi-model ensemble on a one-degree grid averaged to GAUL1 units. Under SSP5-8.5 the average probabilities rise from 10 and 1 percent to 14.6 and 1.9 percent, with large spatial heterogeneity: the 100-year probability becomes 2.2 percent in Tennessee, 2.3 in Michigan and 1.4 in Tokyo, but 0.8 in Tangier. Each firm's locations and capacities are recomputed under the new probabilities, with the choice set extended to all GAUL1 units of countries with car sales. Damage parameters are held fixed and other climate effects are ignored. The spatially correlated version used for robustness draws a latent normal vector with covariance:

Ωii=1    for all i,Ωij=exp⁡(−λ distij)    for all i≠j(26)\Omega_{ii}=1\;\;\text{for all }i,\qquad\Omega_{ij}=\exp(-\lambda\,dist_{ij})\;\;\text{for all }i\neq j \tag{26}Ωii​=1for all i,Ωij​=exp(−λdistij​)for all i=j(26)

and assigns the shock of each location by comparing its latent draw with the thresholds Φ−1(ri)\Phi^{-1}(r_i)Φ−1(ri​) and Φ−1(ri+si)\Phi^{-1}(r_i+s_i)Φ−1(ri​+si​).

  • Plant structure: from the current risk landscape to SSP5-8.5, the average number of plants per firm rises from 6.49 to 6.78 (4.4 percent), capacity per plant falls from 152.9 to 141.9 thousand cars (7.2 percent), and capacity per firm falls from 465.5 to 442.9 thousand (4.9 percent). Without any flood risk the firm would have 7.08 plants and 513.6 thousand units of capacity, all of it used.

  • Spare capacity and concentration: average capacity utilization falls from 95.3 to 93.0 percent, so firms hold 7.0 percent of capacity for hedging. The Herfindahl index of capacity across locations falls from 0.882 to 0.825.

  • Profits and adaptation: average profits fall by 4.1 percent with adaptation and by 5.3 percent when plant configurations are held at their current-risk optimum, so adaptation averts 22.9 percent of the loss (22.9 percent under SSP3-7.0 and 1.4 percent under SSP1-1.9).

  • Geography: global production falls by 6.6 percent and global capacity by 4.9 percent. Production rises in Morocco, Egypt, South Africa, Italy and Mexico and falls in most other countries (7 percent in the United States). Most reallocation is within countries and trading blocs, for example from Michigan and Tennessee toward Nebraska and Kansas, toward the south of Germany, Spain and France, and toward the north of China.

  • Costs and prices: the quantity-weighted average marginal cost rises by 7.4 percent while capacity costs barely change. Car price indices rise in every country, by 2.6 percent on average.

The price effect is decomposed into reorganization and the direct effect of more frequent shocks:

Pj′Pjo=Pj′,nsPjo⋅Pj′Pj′,ns(27)\frac{P_j'}{P_j^o}=\frac{P_j^{',ns}}{P_j^o}\cdot\frac{P_j'}{P_j^{',ns}} \tag{27}Pjo​Pj′​​=Pjo​Pj′,ns​​⋅Pj′,ns​Pj′​​(27)

where PjoP_j^oPjo​ is the baseline price index, Pj′P_j'Pj′​ is the index with new probabilities and adapted plants, and Pj′,nsP_j^{',ns}Pj′,ns​ is the index with adapted plants but baseline shock frequencies. The first ratio, the indirect effect of reorganization, is the main driver. Consistent with this, when firms do not adapt, price indices rise by only 1.0 percent. A back-of-the-envelope conversion gives a consumer surplus loss of 2,489 million dollars with adaptation against 915 million without, and a total welfare loss of 52,751 million with adaptation against 66,858 million without. Consumers are insured against idiosyncratic disruptions of single varieties by substitution across many varieties, whereas firms, with a handful of plants, insure by moving capacity away from the most productive locations and by shrinking, which is an aggregate shock to consumers. The paper runs no explicit policy experiment; it reads this result as a cautionary note for policies that subsidize resilience.

  • Damage size: with damages twice as large (κ1=0.11\kappa_1=0.11κ1​=0.11, κ2=0.21\kappa_2=0.21κ2​=0.21), profits fall by 4.60 percent, utilization falls from 92.9 to 89.2 percent and adaptation averts 27.3 percent of losses. With damages half as large (κ1=0.44\kappa_1=0.44κ1​=0.44, κ2=0.83\kappa_2=0.83κ2​=0.83), profits fall by 1.31 percent, utilization stays above 99 percent, the number of plants falls slightly (6.53 to 6.42) and adaptation averts 9.4 percent.

  • Spatial correlation: with fast decay (λ=0.1\lambda=0.1λ=0.1) results are close to the baseline (profits fall by 4.10 percent and 23.6 percent of losses are averted). With slow decay (λ=0.02\lambda=0.02λ=0.02, a latent correlation of 0.55 at 300 kilometers) adaptation averts 49.9 percent of losses, so the incentive to reorganize is stronger when shocks are spatially correlated.

This is the plant-level building block of the event-study estimator of de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille. Plant iii is first exposed to a flood in period FiF_iFi​, and ℓ\ellℓ counts the quarters elapsed since that date. The first difference, Yi,Fi+ℓ−Yi,Fi−1Y_{i,F_i+\ell}-Y_{i,F_i-1}Yi,Fi​+ℓ​−Yi,Fi​−1​, is the change in the log production of plant iii between the last quarter before its first flood and ℓ\ellℓ quarters after it; since YYY is in logs it is approximately a growth rate. The subtracted term is the average of the same long difference, taken over the same calendar dates, among the plants i′i'i′ that are still untreated at that horizon, that is, with Fi′>Fi+ℓF_{i'}>F_i+\ellFi′​>Fi​+ℓ. The fraction inside the sum is one over the number of such plants and does not depend on the summation index, so the whole term is a simple mean. Writing NiℓntN^{nt}_{i\ell}Niℓnt​ (a symbol not used in the note) for that number, the equation reads

DIDiℓ=(Yi,Fi+ℓ−Yi,Fi−1)−1Niℓnt∑i′:Fi′>Fi+ℓ(Yi′,Fi+ℓ−Yi′,Fi−1)DID_{i\ell}=\left(Y_{i,F_i+\ell}-Y_{i,F_i-1}\right)-\frac{1}{N^{nt}_{i\ell}}\sum_{i':F_{i'}>F_i+\ell}\left(Y_{i',F_i+\ell}-Y_{i',F_i-1}\right)DIDiℓ​=(Yi,Fi​+ℓ​−Yi,Fi​−1​)−Niℓnt​1​i′:Fi′​>Fi​+ℓ∑​(Yi′,Fi​+ℓ​−Yi′,Fi​−1​)

Each DIDiℓDID_{i\ell}DIDiℓ​ is therefore a two-by-two difference-in-differences: one treated plant against a group of not-yet-treated plants, before and after. It measures the effect of the first flood under two assumptions. The first is parallel trends: without the flood, the log production of plant iii would have changed between Fi−1F_i-1Fi​−1 and Fi+ℓF_i+\ellFi​+ℓ by as much as that of the not-yet-treated plants. The second is no anticipation, so that the quarter Fi−1F_i-1Fi​−1 is a clean baseline. A negative value means that the flood lowered production.

The form is chosen because floods arrive at different dates for different plants. A two-way fixed effects regression would then also use already-flooded plants as controls, and with effects that build up over time (the paper finds that they stabilize only after about 20 quarters) those comparisons can receive negative weights. Here the control group never contains a plant that has already been treated. The price is that the control group shrinks as ℓ\ellℓ grows, because 77 percent of plants are eventually treated, so long horizons are estimated less precisely. The plant-level terms are averaged in equation (2). The reallocation result uses the same formula with the treatment redefined as a flood at a sibling plant.

This equation averages the plant-level terms of equation (1) into one number per horizon. The sum runs over the plants whose horizon ℓ\ellℓ falls inside the sample, Fi+ℓ≤TF_i+\ell\leq TFi​+ℓ≤T, and Nℓ1N^1_{\ell}Nℓ1​ is the number of such plants, so every plant receives the same weight:

DID+,ℓ=1Nℓ1∑i:Fi+ℓ≤TDIDiℓDID_{+,\ell}=\frac{1}{N^1_{\ell}}\sum_{i:F_i+\ell\leq T}DID_{i\ell}DID+,ℓ​=Nℓ1​1​i:Fi​+ℓ≤T∑​DIDiℓ​

Under parallel trends and no anticipation, DID+,ℓDID_{+,\ell}DID+,ℓ​ estimates the average effect, on the plants observed at that horizon, of having been flooded for the first time ℓ\ellℓ quarters earlier. The effect includes whatever happens afterwards, later floods included, because the comparison is with plants that have not been flooded at all. Plotting it against ℓ\ellℓ gives the event-study figure, and the same construction for dates before the flood gives the placebo estimates used to judge pre-trends.

Two remarks help in reading the numbers. First, the set of plants changes with ℓ\ellℓ: plants flooded late in the sample contribute only to short horizons, so differences across horizons mix dynamics with composition. Second, the outcome is in logs, so the long-run estimates convert to percentage changes as

e−0.34−1≈−0.29,e−0.69−1≈−0.50,e0.46−1≈0.58e^{-0.34}-1\approx-0.29,\qquad e^{-0.69}-1\approx-0.50,\qquad e^{0.46}-1\approx0.58e−0.34−1≈−0.29,e−0.69−1≈−0.50,e0.46−1≈0.58

that is, a fall of about 29 percent after an average flood, a fall of about one half after a 100-year flood, and a rise of about 58 percent at unflooded sibling plants.

The estimates are used again in the structural part. The damage parameters κ1\kappa_1κ1​ and κ2\kappa_2κ2​ of equation (7) are chosen so that the model-implied fall in the log output of a flooded plant, with capacity held fixed, matches the event-study estimates for 100-year and 10-year floods. Standard errors are clustered by GAUL1 unit because floods hit all plants of a region together.

The second is RjR_jRj​ times the log of a CES aggregate of car varieties; write QCQ_CQC​ for that aggregate, so that the second part is Rjlog⁡QCR_j\log Q_CRj​logQC​ (the outer exponent in the display belongs to the argument of the log). The equation combines a linear technology with a capacity limit. Output QinQ_{in}Qin​ of firm nnn in location iii equals labor LinL_{in}Lin​ times the ex post productivity εin\varepsilon_{in}εin​, and it cannot exceed the installed capacity CinC_{in}Cin​, which is measured in units of output (cars per period). Productivity has three components. The firm component ϕn\phi_nϕn​ and the firm-location component zinz_{in}zin​ are known when capacity is chosen. The weather shock κin\kappa_{in}κin​ of equation (7) is realized afterwards and is at most one.

Producing QQQ units takes Q/εinQ/\varepsilon_{in}Q/εin​ workers paid the wage wiw_iwi​, so the cost function of a plant is

costin(Q)=wiεinQfor 0≤Q≤Cin,and Q>Cin is infeasible\text{cost}_{in}(Q)=\frac{w_i}{\varepsilon_{in}}Q\quad\text{for }0\leq Q\leq C_{in},\qquad\text{and }Q>C_{in}\text{ is infeasible}costin​(Q)=εin​wi​​Qfor 0≤Q≤Cin​,and Q>Cin​ is infeasible

The marginal cost is constant at wi/εinw_i/\varepsilon_{in}wi​/εin​ up to capacity and then becomes infinite, which gives an L-shaped supply curve for each plant. Two modelling choices are worth noting. First, a flood lowers productivity, not capacity: a flooded plant can still produce up to CinC_{in}Cin​, but each unit costs 1/κin1/\kappa_{in}1/κin​ times as much. With the estimates of the paper, unit costs are multiplied by about 4.4 after a 100-year flood and by about 2.4 after a 10-year flood. Second, capacity is the only source of decreasing returns. Without it, a multiplant firm with constant marginal costs would serve each market from one cheapest plant independently of all other markets, and nothing would limit how much production could be moved to a sibling plant after a flood.

The capacity limit is what gives resilience a cost. Moving production away from a flooded plant is possible only if another plant has room, and room has to be paid for in advance. The limit enters the ex post problem (9) as a constraint with multiplier νin\nu_{in}νin​, and the pricing rule (10) shows that the multiplier acts as an addition to the marginal cost wi/εinw_i/\varepsilon_{in}wi​/εin​. Since capacity is continuous and can be zero, the same variable also determines whether a plant exists, as equation (12) shows.

This is the assumed distribution of the weather shock. The shock multiplies productivity in equation (6) and takes three values: κ1\kappa_1κ1​ in a severe (100-year) flood, which has probability rir_iri​; κ2\kappa_2κ2​ in a moderate (10-year) flood, which has probability sis_isi​; and one otherwise. The restrictions κ1<κ2<1\kappa_1<\kappa_2<1κ1​<κ2​<1 and ri<sir_i<s_iri​<si​ say that the rarer event is the more damaging one. The damage sizes are common to all locations and firms; only the probabilities carry a location index. The three outcomes are mutually exclusive, so sis_isi​ is the probability of a moderate flood that is not also a severe one. This matters for the thresholds discussed with equation (26).

The implied mean productivity loss and mean cost increase are

E[κin]=1−ri(1−κ1)−si(1−κ2),E[1κin]=1+ri(1κ1−1)+si(1κ2−1)\mathbb{E}[\kappa_{in}]=1-r_i(1-\kappa_1)-s_i(1-\kappa_2),\qquad\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{\kappa_{in}}\right]=1+r_i\left(\frac{1}{\kappa_1}-1\right)+s_i\left(\frac{1}{\kappa_2}-1\right)E[κin​]=1−ri​(1−κ1​)−si​(1−κ2​),E[κin​1​]=1+ri​(κ1​1​−1)+si​(κ2​1​−1)

With the baseline probabilities ri=0.01r_i=0.01ri​=0.01 and si=0.10s_i=0.10si​=0.10 and the estimates κ1=0.227\kappa_1=0.227κ1​=0.227 and κ2=0.415\kappa_2=0.415κ2​=0.415, expected productivity is about 0.9340.9340.934 and the expected unit cost is about 1.1751.1751.175 times its undisrupted level. Under SSP5-8.5 the average probabilities rise to 0.0190.0190.019 and 0.1460.1460.146, and the same formulas give about 0.9000.9000.900 and 1.2701.2701.270.

A discrete distribution is used for two reasons. It matches the two categories of floods in the event study, so that each damage parameter can be tied to one estimate. And it makes the climate counterfactual simple: climate change is a change in the pair (ri,si)(r_i,s_i)(ri​,si​) for every location, with the damages held fixed. What the assumption rules out is damage that varies with local protection, with the firm, or continuously with flood depth. In the baseline the shocks are independent across locations; equation (26) describes the correlated version. The vector of shocks across the III locations is the state of the world over which the firm takes expectations in equation (11).

This is an accounting identity for the output of a plant under iceberg trade costs. The flow qijnq_{ijn}qijn​ is measured at destination: it is the number of cars of firm nnn that arrive in market jjj from location iii. To deliver one car, τij≥1\tau_{ij}\geq1τij​≥1 cars must be produced, the difference being used up in transport and tariffs. Total production in location iii is therefore the sum of the flows, each multiplied by its trade cost.

The identity has two consequences that the rest of the note uses. Combining it with the technology (6), the labor cost of delivering one car from iii to jjj is

wiεinτij\frac{w_i}{\varepsilon_{in}}\tau_{ij}εin​wi​​τij​

which is the cost term of the ex post problem (9). And combining it with the capacity limit of equation (6) gives the constraint of that problem:

∑j=1Jτijqijn≤Cin\sum_{j=1}^{J}\tau_{ij}q_{ijn}\leq C_{in}j=1∑J​τij​qijn​≤Cin​

A car delivered to a distant market uses up more capacity than a car delivered nearby, by the same factor τij\tau_{ij}τij​ by which it uses more labor. This is why, in the pricing rule (10), the trade cost multiplies the sum of the marginal cost and the shadow value of capacity and not the marginal cost alone.

Trade costs do not depend on the firm, and they are parameterized in equation (22) as a function of tariffs and distance. Because any plant can ship to any market, each plant is a potential export platform, and it is this feature that allows a sibling plant to replace a flooded one. As a numerical illustration, with τij=1.2\tau_{ij}=1.2τij​=1.2 and a capacity of 120 thousand cars, a plant that serves only market jjj can deliver at most 100 thousand cars there.

A flood at plant iii raises wi/εinw_i/\varepsilon_{in}wi​/εin​; markets switch to other plants, whose multipliers rise, and the price increases in every market those plants serve, including markets that never bought from the flooded plant.

This is the first-stage problem. The firm chooses a nonnegative capacity for each of the III locations before the weather shocks are known. The first term is the expectation, over the joint distribution of the productivity vector εn\boldsymbol{\varepsilon_n}εn​, of the operating profits defined in equation (9). Given the known components ϕn\phi_nϕn​ and zinz_{in}zin​, the only randomness is the vector of shocks of equation (7). The second term is the cost of capacity, linear in the baseline with marginal cost αin\alpha_{in}αin​; in general it is ∑ifin(Cin)\sum_if_{in}(C_{in})∑i​fin​(Cin​) with each function convex. The problem is static: capacity is chosen once and its cost is to be read as a per-period cost.

Three features of the formulation matter. First, there are no fixed costs and no integer variables. Whether to open a plant and how large to make it are one continuous decision, and a location with zero capacity is a location without a plant. Because the marginal cost of the first unit is strictly positive, zeros arise naturally; equation (12) gives the condition. Second, the firm is risk neutral. Diversification does not come from aversion to risk but from the shape of operating profits, which are concave in capacities (equation (13)) and in which the value of capacity in one location depends on the shocks in all others. Third, the choice is made once for all states, while production in problem (9) adapts to each state. Capacity is therefore the link between states of the world: a unit installed in location iii is available in every state, valuable in some and idle in others.

Without uncertainty the problem collapses to a standard one. Every installed unit is used, the multiplier of each open plant equals αin\alpha_{in}αin​, and the firm behaves as if the marginal cost of producing in location iii were

wiεin+αin\frac{w_i}{\varepsilon_{in}}+\alpha_{in}εin​wi​​+αin​

which is the multinational production model with constant marginal costs. The block for equation (12) derives this. In the quantitative model the expectation is replaced by an average over simulated states (equation (14)) and the problem is solved through its dual (equations (16) and (17)).

Two implications follow at once. An expectation is a weighted sum with nonnegative weights and preserves concavity, and subtracting a convex cost preserves it too, so the objective of problem (11) is concave on the convex set of nonnegative capacities. Any local maximum is then global and the conditions of equation (12) are sufficient. The economic content is diminishing returns to capacity: the flows that are optimal under two capacity plans can always be mixed, and mixing them under the mixed plan earns at least the average profit. In a fixed-cost model this argument fails, because the average of two plant configurations pays a fixed cost for every plant that either of them opens.

The equation replaces an expectation by a simulation average. The state of the world is the vector of shocks across all locations, and with three possible values per location (equation (7)) there are 3I3^I3I states, far too many to enumerate when the locations are the first-level administrative units of all car-selling countries. The result is the program in the note: a linear objective, linear inequality constraints and one three-dimensional cone constraint per market and state. The optimal νins\nu_{ins}νins​ are the state-contingent shadow values, the optimal μjns\mu_{jns}μjns​ give prices through equation (10), and the multipliers of the first group of constraints are the optimal capacities, as shown in the derivation of equation (16).

A remark on the first constraint. The statement of Proposition 3 in the paper prints its right-hand side as fin′(Cin)f_{in}'(C_{in})fin′​(Cin​). The proposition reformulates the dual of Proposition 2, which is derived for the linear cost fin(Cin)=αinCinf_{in}(C_{in})=\alpha_{in}C_{in}fin​(Cin​)=αin​Cin​, and the proof in the paper's appendix carries the constraint as

1S∑s=1Sνins≤αin∀i\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\nu_{ins}\leq\alpha_{in}\quad\forall iS1​s=1∑S​νins​≤αin​∀i

This is the form used in the note. Capacity is not a variable of the dual program (it is the multiplier of this very constraint), so a right-hand side that depends on CinC_{in}Cin​ is not a well-defined constant; the two forms coincide only because marginal cost is the constant αin\alpha_{in}αin​ in the linear case. For a nonlinear cost the dual has a different objective, with an extra term coming from the conjugate of the cost function, and the paper treats that case separately or through the two-step method of equation (19).

This is the definition of the three-dimensional power cone, the standard set used by conic solvers to represent power functions. A point x=(x1,x2,x3)x=(x_1,x_2,x_3)x=(x1​,x2​,x3​) belongs to the cone when its first two coordinates are nonnegative and their weighted geometric mean, with weights α\alphaα and 1−α1-\alpha1−α for some α\alphaα between zero and one, is at least the absolute value of the third coordinate. The exponent α\alphaα is a generic parameter of the cone and has nothing to do with the capacity cost αin\alpha_{in}αin​. The set is a cone because the inequality is homogeneous of degree one: scaling a point by a positive number keeps it in the set.

In equation (17) the cone is used with α=1/σ\alpha=1/\sigmaα=1/σ and with the point (tjns,μjns,1)(t_{jns},\mu_{jns},1)(tjns​,μjns​,1), where it expresses the epigraph of a negative power:

t1σμ1−1σ≥1⟺t≥μ−1−1/σ1/σ=μ1−σt^{\frac{1}{\sigma}}\mu^{1-\frac{1}{\sigma}}\geq1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad t\geq\mu^{-\frac{1-1/\sigma}{1/\sigma}}=\mu^{1-\sigma}tσ1​μ1−σ1​≥1⟺t≥μ−1/σ1−1/σ​=μ1−σ

With the estimate σ=2.6\sigma=2.6σ=2.6 the two exponents are about 0.3850.3850.385 and 0.6150.6150.615, and the constraint is t≥μ−1.6t\geq\mu^{-1.6}t≥μ−1.6.

The set is convex. For the slice used here this can be checked directly. Take two points with to≥(μo)1−σt^o\geq(\mu^o)^{1-\sigma}to≥(μo)1−σ and t′≥(μ′)1−σt'\geq(\mu')^{1-\sigma}t′≥(μ′)1−σ and a weight θ\thetaθ between zero and one. Adding the two inequalities with weights, and then using the convexity of the function x1−σx^{1-\sigma}x1−σ on positive numbers,

θto+(1−θ)t′≥θ(μo)1−σ+(1−θ)(μ′)1−σ≥(θμo+(1−θ)μ′)1−σ\theta t^o+(1-\theta)t'\geq\theta(\mu^o)^{1-\sigma}+(1-\theta)(\mu')^{1-\sigma}\geq\left(\theta\mu^o+(1-\theta)\mu'\right)^{1-\sigma}θto+(1−θ)t′≥θ(μo)1−σ+(1−θ)(μ′)1−σ≥(θμo+(1−θ)μ′)1−σ

so the averaged point satisfies the constraint as well. In general the cone is convex because a weighted geometric mean is a concave function on the nonnegative orthant.

Writing the constraint in this form is what makes the problem tractable. A solver such as Mosek does not treat the constraint as a generic nonlinear function; it has a dedicated interior-point method for power cones, with the same polynomial-time guarantees as for linear programs. The whole ex ante problem of a firm, with thousands of states, is thus solved as one conic program and without any search over sets of locations.

The objective has a clear reading. Raising a multiplier increases the first part and lowers the second, and the minimum balances them. which is the capacity constraint with complementary slackness.

That is why this formulation works for any convex cost. The same two substitutions as in equation (17) turn it into a small conic program. Each formula is the unconstrained monopoly quantity of equation (10), multiplied by τ\tauτ to convert sales into capacity, for a plant whose marginal cost is its production cost plus the capacity cost divided by the probability that the capacity is used. A higher ppp raises the effective cost of plant 1 and lowers that of plant 2. Plant 2 is pure spare capacity: it is idle with probability 1−p1-p1−p.

The note states the maintained assumption in words; in terms of parameters it requires two inequalities, which neither the note nor the paper writes out. Plant 2 is idle in the normal state when marginal revenue at C1∗C_1^*C1∗​ is below its delivered cost, and plant 1 is idle in the disrupted state when marginal revenue at C2∗C_2^*C2∗​ is below its delivered cost there. They say that capacity is cheap relative to the productivity gaps. The second fails when ppp is small, since its left-hand side grows without bound as ppp goes to zero; then the solution is of a different type (plant 2 is not built, or the disrupted plant 1 is used alongside it), and the closed form no longer applies. This is why the paper turns to numerical solutions for the comparative statics.

Start from the pricing rule (10) for a car model mmm that is assembled in plant iii and sold in market jjj. Conditional on the observed origin, the minimum is attained at iii, and the price is a constant markup over the augmented delivered cost. Writing mcimmc_{im}mcim​ (a symbol not used in the note) for the production cost of the model in that plant plus the shadow value of the plant's capacity,

pijm=σσ−1τij mcimp_{ijm}=\frac{\sigma}{\sigma-1}\tau_{ij}\,mc_{im}pijm​=σ−1σ​τij​mcim​

Take logs and substitute the parameterization of trade costs, τij=(1+tariffij)ϕtardijϕdist\tau_{ij}=(1+\text{tariff}_{ij})^{\phi_{tar}}d_{ij}^{\phi_{dist}}τij​=(1+tariffij​)ϕtar​dijϕdist​​:

log⁡pijm=ϕtarlog⁡(1+tariffij)+ϕdistlog⁡dij+log⁡σσ−1+log⁡mcim⏟αim\log p_{ijm}=\phi_{tar}\log(1+\text{tariff}_{ij})+\phi_{dist}\log d_{ij}+\underbrace{\log\frac{\sigma}{\sigma-1}+\log mc_{im}}_{\alpha_{im}}logpijm​=ϕtar​log(1+tariffij​)+ϕdist​logdij​+αim​logσ−1σ​+logmcim​​​

The last two terms do not vary across destinations and are collected in the model-plant fixed effect αim\alpha_{im}αim​. Adding a destination effect αj\alpha_jαj​ and an error uijmu_{ijm}uijm​ gives the estimating equation. Here αim\alpha_{im}αim​ and αj\alpha_jαj​ are fixed effects and are unrelated to the capacity cost αin\alpha_{in}αin​.

The step that matters is that the shadow value of capacity is absorbed by the fixed effect. This is a prediction of the model: the multiplier of a plant is common to all the markets it serves, so although marginal cost is not constant and moves with demand everywhere, it cancels in a comparison of the same model from the same plant across destinations. The trade cost parameters are therefore identified without solving the model, from how the list price of a given model-plant pair varies with the tariff and the distance it faces in different markets. The destination effect absorbs market-wide price differences such as taxes and reporting conventions; the paper describes it as market-specific measurement error. The argument takes the markup to be the same across the destinations of a model-plant pair, which the constant-elasticity demand delivers.

The coefficients are elasticities of the price with respect to one plus the tariff and to distance. The estimate ϕtar=0.834\phi_{tar}=0.834ϕtar​=0.834 means that a tariff higher by 10 percent of the price raises the delivered price by about 8.3 percent, and ϕdist=0.033\phi_{dist}=0.033ϕdist​=0.033 means that doubling distance raises it by about 0.033×log⁡20.033\times\log20.033×log2, or 2.3 percent. The fitted trade costs enter the firm's problem (9) and the quantity regression (24).

The two regressions come from a nested CES demand system: models of a brand are combined into a brand composite with elasticity σm\sigma_mσm​, and brand composites are combined with the elasticity σ\sigmaσ of equation (3).

Two points of interpretation. First, the brand effect and the home dummy identify (σ−1)log⁡ψjn(\sigma-1)\log\psi_{jn}(σ−1)logψjn​, as the note states; under the linear demand display printed in the paper they would be read as log⁡ψjn\log\psi_{jn}logψjn​, and the two readings differ by the factor σ−1≈1.6\sigma-1\approx1.6σ−1≈1.6. Second, a home coefficient of about 1.0 means that a brand's sales in its home market are e1.0≈2.7e^{1.0}\approx2.7e1.0≈2.7 times what its price and quality would predict elsewhere. The nesting is needed because the data are at the level of car models while a firm in the model sells one variety; the inner regression supplies the price index that collapses models into one brand-level price.

Start from the quantity rule (10). Conditional on the observed origin iii, the minimum is attained there, and with mcimmc_{im}mcim​ the production cost plus the shadow value of capacity as in the block for equation (22),

The regression is a gravity equation at the level of a model, an assembly plant and a destination. The object of interest is the destination effect δj\delta_jδj​: it is the part of market size that is common to all firms, namely expenditure on cars and the price index, which could not be obtained from the share regression (23) because prices are observed in only seven countries, whereas quantities are observed everywhere. As in equation (22), the model-plant effect absorbs the unobserved marginal cost including the shadow value of capacity, so the regression can be run without solving the model; δj\delta_jδj​ is identified by comparing the sales of the same model from the same plant across destinations, after removing trade costs, the brand effect and the home effect.

Three remarks. The coefficients on tariffs and distance are written as free parameters; the model implies the values −2.6×0.834≈−2.2-2.6\times0.834\approx-2.2−2.6×0.834≈−2.2 and −2.6×0.033≈−0.09-2.6\times0.033\approx-0.09−2.6×0.033≈−0.09, so the equation as written does not impose the first-step estimates. The derivation is conditional on the observed sourcing: when a market is served by several plants the rule (10) determines the total sold in the market and not each flow, and the regression treats each observed flow as following the same log-linear form. And the equation is applied to models although the theory is written for a brand; the inner nest of equation (23) is what connects the two levels. The recovered δj\delta_jδj​, the brand effects and the home coefficient together give the market sizes βjn\beta_{jn}βjn​ that enter problem (9).

The equation states the distributional assumptions for the two unobserved firm-location primitives: the productivity zinz_{in}zin​ of equation (6) and the marginal capacity cost αin\alpha_{in}αin​ of equation (11). Each is log-normal, which keeps it positive, with a location parameter that is linear in observables and a dispersion parameter common to all firms and locations. Draws are independent across firms and locations conditional on the observables. Reading the dispersion parameters as standard deviations of the logs (the paper does not say whether they are standard deviations or variances), the assumption can be written with standard normal errors einze^z_{in}einz​ and einαe^{\alpha}_{in}einα​, symbols not used in the note:

log⁡zin=Xin′δz+Gi′δw+ξzeinz,log⁡αin=Xin′δα+ξαeinα\log z_{in}=X_{in}'\delta^z+G_i'\delta^w+\xi^ze^z_{in},\qquad\log\alpha_{in}=X_{in}'\delta^{\alpha}+\xi^{\alpha}e^{\alpha}_{in}logzin​=Xin′​δz+Gi′​δw+ξzeinz​,logαin​=Xin′​δα+ξαeinα​

The vector XinX_{in}Xin​ holds firm-location observables and GiG_iGi​ holds dummies for country income groups. The income-group term appears only in the productivity equation. It stands in for wages: in problem (9) only the ratio wi/εinw_i/\varepsilon_{in}wi​/εin​ matters, so wage differences cannot be separated from productivity differences and are absorbed in δw\delta^wδw.

A distribution is needed because the model cannot be inverted. Most firm-location pairs have no plant, and for them the first-order condition (12) is an inequality that only bounds the primitives. Where there is a plant, one observed output would have to reveal two unobservables. The parameters are therefore estimated by simulated method of moments: draw the two primitives for every firm and location, solve the conic program (17), and match moments of plant locations and sizes. Separate identification comes from the two margins. Productivity mostly governs whether a location has a plant, and capacity cost mostly governs how large the plant is, since plants are often capacity constrained and the capacity formula (21) shows the direct role of αin\alpha_{in}αin​.

Coefficients on log regressors are elasticities, and coefficients on dummies are log differences. The home coefficients of −0.277-0.277−0.277 for capacity costs and 0.2270.2270.227 for productivity convert to

e−0.277−1≈−0.24,e0.227−1≈0.25e^{-0.277}-1\approx-0.24,\qquad e^{0.227}-1\approx0.25e−0.277−1≈−0.24,e0.227−1≈0.25

so capacity is about 24 percent cheaper at home (28 log points) and productivity about 25 percent higher. The estimated dispersions are small, so the variation in the two primitives is driven almost entirely by the observables, and with a normal error the median of each primitive is the exponential of its linear index.

The equation defines the covariance matrix of a latent normal vector used to generate flood shocks that are correlated across space. Each location has a latent variable, written uin∗u^*_{in}uin∗​ in the paper, and the vector of latent variables is multivariate normal with mean zero and covariance matrix Ω\OmegaΩ. The diagonal entries are one, so each latent variable is standard normal and the off-diagonal entries are correlations. The correlation between two locations decays exponentially with the distance distijdist_{ij}distij​ between their centroids at rate λ\lambdaλ; in this equation jjj indexes a second location and not a market. A larger λ\lambdaλ means faster decay, and as λ\lambdaλ grows without bound the shocks become independent, which is the baseline. The exponential kernel guarantees that the matrix is a valid, positive definite covariance matrix.

The latent variable is turned into the three-valued shock of equation (7) by two thresholds Zi1<Zi2Z^1_i<Z^2_iZi1​<Zi2​:

κin={κ1if uin∗≤Zi1κ2if Zi1<uin∗≤Zi21if uin∗>Zi2\kappa_{in}=\begin{cases}\kappa_1&\text{if }u^*_{in}\leq Z^1_i\\\kappa_2&\text{if }Z^1_i<u^*_{in}\leq Z^2_i\\1&\text{if }u^*_{in}>Z^2_i\end{cases}κin​=⎩⎨⎧​κ1​κ2​1​if uin∗​≤Zi1​if Zi1​<uin∗​≤Zi2​if uin∗​>Zi2​​

The thresholds must reproduce the marginal probabilities of equation (7). Since the latent variable is standard normal with distribution function Φ\PhiΦ,

Pr⁡(κin=κ1)=Φ(Zi1)=ri,Pr⁡(κin=κ2)=Φ(Zi2)−Φ(Zi1)=si\Pr(\kappa_{in}=\kappa_1)=\Phi(Z^1_i)=r_i,\qquad\Pr(\kappa_{in}=\kappa_2)=\Phi(Z^2_i)-\Phi(Z^1_i)=s_iPr(κin​=κ1​)=Φ(Zi1​)=ri​,Pr(κin​=κ2​)=Φ(Zi2​)−Φ(Zi1​)=si​

and solving these two equations gives

Zi1=Φ−1(ri),Zi2=Φ−1(ri+si)Z^1_i=\Phi^{-1}(r_i),\qquad Z^2_i=\Phi^{-1}(r_i+s_i)Zi1​=Φ−1(ri​),Zi2​=Φ−1(ri​+si​)

These are the thresholds stated in the note. The paper's appendix prints the second threshold as Φ−1(si)\Phi^{-1}(s_i)Φ−1(si​). With that threshold the probability of the moderate shock is si−ris_i-r_isi​−ri​ and not sis_isi​: at the baseline values it would be 9 percent in place of 10 percent, and the probability of no shock would be 90 percent in place of 89 percent. The threshold Φ−1(si)\Phi^{-1}(s_i)Φ−1(si​) would be right only if sis_isi​ were the probability of exceeding the 10-year threshold, severe events included, which is how the climate data are constructed but not how equation (7) defines it. Given equation (7), the correct second threshold is Φ−1(ri+si)\Phi^{-1}(r_i+s_i)Φ−1(ri​+si​).

There is also an unstated unit convention. With distance in kilometers, λ=0.02\lambda=0.02λ=0.02 would give a latent correlation of e−6≈0.002e^{-6}\approx0.002e−6≈0.002 at 300 kilometers. The reported values, 0.550.550.55 at 300 kilometers for λ=0.02\lambda=0.02λ=0.02 and 0.050.050.05 for λ=0.1\lambda=0.1λ=0.1, are e−0.6e^{-0.6}e−0.6 and e−3e^{-3}e−3, so distance must be measured in units of 10 kilometers. The correlation between the discrete shocks is lower than between the latent variables (the paper reports 0.290.290.29 against 0.550.550.55), because thresholding discards information. Spatial correlation matters economically because it makes nearby plants poor substitutes for each other in bad states: hedging requires capacity farther away, which is why adaptation averts a larger share of losses when correlation decays slowly.

The equation splits the change in the car price index of market jjj into two factors. It is an identity: the intermediate index cancels between the numerator of the first ratio and the denominator of the second. Three equilibria are compared. The baseline index PjoP_j^oPjo​ has plants chosen optimally for current flood probabilities and shocks drawn with those probabilities. The index Pj′P_j'Pj′​ has plants chosen for the future probabilities and shocks drawn with the future probabilities. The intermediate index Pj′,nsP_j^{',ns}Pj′,ns​ has plants chosen for the future probabilities but shocks drawn with the current ones. Each index is computed from equation (5) with the prices of equation (10).

The first ratio therefore changes only the location and capacity of plants and keeps the frequency of floods fixed: it is the indirect effect of reorganization. The second ratio keeps plants fixed at their adapted configuration and changes only the frequency of floods: it is the direct effect. In logs the decomposition is additive:

log⁡Pj′Pjo=log⁡Pj′,nsPjo+log⁡Pj′Pj′,ns\log\frac{P_j'}{P_j^o}=\log\frac{P_j^{',ns}}{P_j^o}+\log\frac{P_j'}{P_j^{',ns}}logPjo​Pj′​​=logPjo​Pj′,ns​​+logPj′,ns​Pj′​​

The left-hand side is about 0.0260.0260.026 on average. The paper finds that the first term accounts for most of it. The reason is that adaptation moves capacity toward locations that are safer but less productive or more expensive, and reduces total capacity, which raises the augmented marginal cost in equation (10) in every state, including states without any flood.

The decomposition is not unique, because the two changes interact. One could change the shock frequencies first, with plants at their baseline configuration, and reorganize afterwards. Writing Pjo,sP_j^{o,s}Pjo,s​ (a symbol not used in the note) for the index with baseline plants and future frequencies,

Pj′Pjo=Pjo,sPjo⋅Pj′Pjo,s\frac{P_j'}{P_j^o}=\frac{P_j^{o,s}}{P_j^o}\cdot\frac{P_j'}{P_j^{o,s}}Pjo​Pj′​​=Pjo​Pjo,s​​⋅Pjo,s​Pj′​​

Here the first ratio is the price effect when firms do not adapt, which the note reports as 1.01.01.0 percent, so the second ratio, the effect of adaptation given the new climate, is about 1.61.61.6 percent. Both orderings lead to the same conclusion: adaptation raises prices. This is the source of the welfare result. By the indirect utility shown in the block for equation (3), consumer surplus in market jjj changes by

ΔCSj=−Rjlog⁡Pj′Pjo\Delta CS_j=-R_j\log\frac{P_j'}{P_j^o}ΔCSj​=−Rj​logPjo​Pj′​​

so consumers lose more with adaptation than without it, while firms lose less.
